body_markdown:
Amsterdam has gained a bit of a reputation. Contrary to popular belief, it’s nothing to do with the red light district or the herby smell you might catch when walking through certain streets. Rather, it’s the infrastructure.


Once choked by traffic, like many cities Amsterdam made a concerted push in the 1970s and ’80s to transition away from cars and into other methods of transportation—most notably cycling, but also trams and buses.


How different things could have been. Amsterdam is undoubtedly a more pleasant city for not prioritizing cars, but in the early 1970s the method for dealing with rising oil prices and cloying traffic wasn’t as obvious as it seems in retrospect, and it briefly spawned an alternative transportation method: the Witkar.


Wikimedia Commons/Fotograaf Onbekend/Anefo


Witkar—Dutch for “white car,” because all the cars were, well, white—was conceived as an early example of what we know today as a car-sharing service.


Car-sharing works on the premise that not everyone needs to own a car, but some people may still need to drive one occasionally. In a modern context—think ZipCar, Getaround, or the defunct Car2Go—that means branded cars scattered throughout cities that you can source, book, unlock, and drive using an app, before returning them to a parking space for the next person to use. Dozens of people can potentially benefit from being able to use a single car, without having to stump up the ownership costs, and without cities having to find space for all those extra vehicles.


Most modern car-sharing services simply buy in fleets of existing vehicles, though it’s not unusual for such services to use something specifically designed for the purpose. The Autolib’ car-sharing program set up in Paris in 2011 used a vehicle called the Bolloré Bluecar, an all-electric city car designed by Pininfarina, and a nice idea other than Parisian driving and parking standards, and then vandalism, quickly reducing the fleet to scruffy jalopies.


Dutch industrial designer and inventor Luud Schimmelpennink driving a Witkar in March 1973.


Getty Images


You probably wouldn’t have wanted to get into a Parisian-style scrape with the Witkar. Conceived in 1968 by Dutch industrial designer and politician Luud Schimmelpennink, Witkar took the form of a two-seat, fully electric microcar that was notably taller than it was wide or long, and indeed shorter than it was wide, with passengers effectively sitting in an upright glass tube. It was relatively heavy, too, at least for its size, at around 1325 pounds, in part a result of the bank of nickel cadmium batteries that supplied a mere 6.2 miles of range and a 20-mph top speed.


Range wasn’t deemed much of an issue, though. More than 4000 people paid the 25 guilder fee (around $10 then and $50 today) to join the Witkar program when it opened in 1974. Statistics suggested that most people were only covering around 3.1 miles per journey, before parking at a station where overhead conductors recharged the batteries in an admirably quick 10 minutes, ready for the next driver.


To access the cars, each Witkar member received a little plastic key with an embedded sensor for their 25 guilders; pretty sophisticated for the mid 1970s. When they arrived at a station, they’d tap in their destination station using a keypad, and wave the key over a sensor, before driving off. A central computer registered the key, car, and station, and charged each driver accordingly, which typically worked out around one guilder, or ¢40 ($2.10 in 2026), per trip.


That said, part of the limited distance drivers were covering was down to there being only five stations for the 35 cars. Ten more stations were planned by the end of 1976, for a fleet of 100 *Witkarren* , and eventually 1400 cars, but predictably, that never materialized.


Witkars at a charging station, ready for rental.


www.nationaalarchief.nl


Luud Schimmelpennik hoped to sell his Witkar idea outside of Amsterdam, but it never took off.


Getty Images


The way the cars drove probably didn’t help. Chris Goffey, trying out a Witkar for *Autocar* magazine in 1976, described how it was “simple in the extreme,” with a lever for forward, reverse, and park, two pedals, and a steering wheel, but that it had “extremely sensitive steering \[and\] a rather top heavy, unstable feel” for a “\[not\] completely reassuring sensation to the driver.” Goffey did note that other drivers and pedestrians were generally friendly toward Witkar drivers, though.


But he also suggested that, with a widespread tram network and the plans for an underground railway system (the latter starting up in 1977), Witkar demand might never reach fever pitch. Given that cars weren’t shunned back then as they increasingly are in the modern city, you’d have to really buy into the relatively minimal benefits of the Witkar (and its goofy styling) to take one over the relatively low ownership costs (including, at the time, mostly free parking) of a regular economy car. There was also an issue with some stations ending up with an excess of Witkars, and others with none, which clearly reduced its convenience.


“Unless they ban all traffic except electric vehicles from large areas of the city centre,” Goffey wrote, “there doesn’t seem to be much of a future for the concept.”


Nationaal Archief


In many ways, he was on the money. The trams and metro did take over, and in the 1980s Amsterdam quickly ramped up cycling as the primary method of getting around. Witkar soldiered on until 1986 but never grew beyond those original 35 cars and 4000 users, and one imagines usage tailed off pretty quickly through the decade.


If you want to see a Witkar today, there are examples in some museums in the Netherlands, most notably in the[Louwman Museum](https://www.louwmanmuseum.nl/en) on the outskirts of The Hague. Driving one, however, might prove more difficult.


In one respect, though, the spirit of the Witkar lives on. Walk around Amsterdam today and, while bicycles and bags of refuse seem to vie for space on the city’s pavements and parking spaces, one other type of vehicle remains wildly popular: microcars. Spearheaded by the home-built two-seat Canta microcar, which were originally designed for disabled drivers, the compact vehicles are frequently allowed to traverse cycle paths and seem to be parkable more or less anywhere.


Wikimedia Commons/JLPC


Wikimedia Commons/Mario Roberto Duran Ortiz


The Pininfarina-styled Bolloré Bluecar (left) was an all-electric city car for Paris, while the tiny Canta is still in use around Amsterdam.


The Canta is tiny, just over 3.5 feet wide, which is narrower than the Witkar (though looking less like a smoothie maker), but it’s far from the only microcar on the city’s streets. Many are of a slightly different format, conforming to Europe’s heavy quadricycle standards, weighing in at 990 pounds or so and still taking up minimal space on the road.


Citroën’s Ami and its[Fiat Topolino](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/news-articles/mon-ami-italien-french-city-car-spawns-new-fiat-topolino/) equivalent are particularly popular, whirring silently around and taking up minimal space while driving or while parked, and each gives Dutch drivers a four-wheeled alternative to the predominantly two-wheeled transport. They’re at least a small window into what life might have been like had Witkar succeeded.
